name: R-1,3-butanediol

card.summary: A diol the body converts into the ketone beta-hydroxybutyrate; human evidence for appearance or fat loss is not established in the sources.
card.note: Do not confuse with 1,4-butanediol, which converts to GHB.

quick.overview:
R-1,3-butanediol is the (R) form of a four-carbon diol that appears in the exogenous ketone literature as a precursor of beta-hydroxybutyrate. It is also a component of some ketone esters.
Its place in the fat-loss category rests on the idea that raising ketones may affect hunger or metabolism. No trial has tested it for fat loss or appearance.
quick.mechanism: Wikipedia's ketone ester article states that R-1,3-butanediol raises blood ketones, by about 60 percent relative to the monoester according to that page. Wikipedia also notes exogenous ketones lower blood glucose and may reduce ghrelin, with insulin's role unclear.
quick.risks: 1,3-butanediol is recognized by the US FDA as a safe food ingredient (21 CFR 172.712) per Wikipedia. Pure chemical hazard notes include eye irritation. A study of a ketone diester in professional cyclists reported impaired time-trial performance.

lead: 1,3-Butanediol (C4H10O2) is a diol and secondary alcohol, a bittersweet water-soluble liquid used as a solvent, flavor-additive carrier, and intermediate for resins. The (R) enantiomer has CAS number 6290-03-5.[1] In the exogenous ketone field, R-1,3-butanediol is described as a compound that significantly raises blood ketone levels and is a component of ketone esters developed at the NIH by Richard Veech and Todd King.[2]

In looksmaxxing and fat-loss circles it is of interest as a route to ketone bodies without a strict ketogenic diet: the body converts it to beta-hydroxybutyrate, and people who use ketone drinks hope for reduced hunger and a leaner physique as part of a cut. Wikipedia's ketone ester article notes that exogenous ketone drinks have been reported to lower the hunger hormone ghrelin.[2] A 2023 crossover trial in 18 adults with prediabetes tested a ketone monoester drink built on R-1,3-butanediol and found ketones rose quickly but ghrelin, PYY and self-reported hunger did not differ significantly from placebo.[9]

The US FDA recognizes 1,3-butanediol as a safe food ingredient under 21 CFR 172.712.[1] The Wikipedia article describes preliminary study of it for exercise recovery and as a possible oral ketone agent in anorexia nervosa research, but states that high production cost limits adoption.[1]
infobox: Recognized as a food ingredient (21 CFR 172.712)

paras: 1,3-Butanediol is made by aldol condensation of acetaldehyde followed by catalytic hydrogenation, and it occurs naturally in bell peppers. Without an R or S label the compound is racemic.[1]

Wikipedia's ketone ester article lists R-1,3-butanediol among exogenous ketone agents, says it should not be confused with 1,4-butanediol (which converts to GHB), and notes that racemic diesters of the compound were tested in deep-sea divers and that C6 and C8 diesters with it are sold by Juvenescence Labs.[2] Exogenous ketones are reported to lower blood glucose and may reduce ghrelin.[2]

Ketone esters were first developed at the NIH by Richard Veech and Todd King and later commercialised by companies including KetoneAid and TdeltaS, and, previously, HVMN, per Wikipedia.[2] The (R) form should not be confused with 1,4-butanediol, which converts to GHB; the two are distinct compounds.[2] Alkane diols, including butanediols, also appear in cosmetics as solvents, and a 2024 expert-panel safety assessment covered ten of them, judging seven safe at current uses and finding data insufficient for three, including 1,4-butanediol.[10]

The same Wikipedia article reports that R-1,3-butanediol was tested once for sports performance and that time to fatigue was not significantly different.[2] A 2017 study of a ketone diester in professional cyclists reported impaired time-trial performance.[3] A registered healthy-volunteer study compared the effects of different ketone supplements on blood beta-hydroxybutyrate and glucose.[4] Registered trials of ketone supplementation in frailty, alcohol use disorder and sleep apnea are under way or suspended; none concerns appearance.[5][6]

The 2023 appetite trial was a randomised crossover design: 18 adults with prediabetes drank a ketone monoester drink or placebo after an overnight fast, with blood sampled over 150 minutes. Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate rose significantly within 30 minutes, but overall ghrelin, PYY and self-reported hunger did not differ significantly, and the authors concluded that acute ketosis did not affect appetite regulation in this group.[9]

Animal work with ketone esters includes a mouse study reporting increased brown adipose tissue mitochondrial biogenesis and UCP1 on a ketone ester diet, and a 2014 mouse study of ketone supplementation in metastatic cancer.[7][8] These are not human appearance outcomes.

chain: R-1,3-butanediol is converted in the body to the ketone beta-hydroxybutyrate
Blood ketones rise, with reported effects on glucose and possibly ghrelin
Possible reduction in hunger during a diet, supporting leaner body composition
angle.text: People who add ketone drinks to a cutting phase do so hoping for steadier appetite and ketosis without eating a strict ketogenic diet. Human trials of appetite have so far reported no significant change in one prediabetes study.
